title: I quit my marketing job to walk dogs for 4 months: It's 'one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had'
description: One early morning in 2022, I found myself watching a dog walker on TikTok and thinking: I want her job.It felt ridiculous. I was finishing up my MBA a
body: One early morning in 2022, I found myself watching a dog walker on TikTok and thinking: I want her job.It felt ridiculous. I was finishing up my MBA and navigating the next chapter of my career with a focus on prestige and financial success. But soon after relocating from Kentucky to California in October 2021, I burned out. I had transitioned into a remote healthcare marketing role, living on the West Coast but still working East Coast hours and completing my second year of business school from afar. While everyone around me seemed to be heading to the beach and enjoying the sunshine, I spent my days inside, glued to a computer screen.The dog walker I followed online seemed to have everything I was craving: fresh air, movement, flexibility and a job that didn't revolve around emails and Zoom meetings.During a long drive, I joked with my husband, "I think I'm going to quit my job and walk dogs." The joke quickly became a plan.My season as a professional dog walkerWithin the span of just a few weeks in the spring of 2022, I quit my job, graduated from business school, traveled to Europe for an old roommate's wedding and then flew to Texas to speak at the Latino Franchise Symposium. While I was there, I created my Rover profile. I highlighted my experience volunteering at animal shelters in college, pet sitting for friends and caring for animals throughout my life.Before I even made it back home to California, I had my first meet-and-greet scheduled with a potential client. Shortly after, I landed my first booking. I was thrilled.At first, I intentionally priced my services below what seemed typical in my area to build reviews, charging about $15 for a drop-in visit and about $17 for a 30-minute walk. Some days I had just one client. I was able to start small because I had savings to tide me over, along with a partner whose job provided steady income and benefits.My goal was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.Courtesy of Sally SimmonsStill, I treated it like a real business from day one. I accepted nearly every opportunity that came my way, taking dogs on midday walks, housesitting on weekends and boarding dogs in my apartment.I sent thoughtful updates to the dog owners filled with photos, detailed notes and plenty of emojis. I shared bathroom break tallies, funny moments and anything unusual they should know. If I stayed overnight, I brought in packages, cleaned up after myself and made sure their home looked exactly as they had left it.My goal wasn't simply to complete the booking. It was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.The reviews started rolling in. As my profile gained traction, I gradually increased my rates, eventually charging $23 for a drop-in visit and $84 for overnight stays. By the time I left the platform four months later, I had earned a five-star rating with 30 reviews, built a roster of recurring clients and filled my calendar.Walking dogs gave me space to think and reflect on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.Christina Locopo | CNBC Make It; Courtesy of Sally SimmonsOne of my favorite memories came when a family asked me to care for their dogs during their wedding weekend. I spent two and a half days at a beautiful resort and dressed the dogs in tiny tuxedos before they walked down the aisle.It reminded me that this work was about helping families enjoy some of the biggest moments of their lives with peace of mind. Years later, we're still friends. They now have a daughter, and my daughter and I recently attended her first birthday party.A new definition of successSome days I walked more than eight miles, logging over 18,000 steps as I explored neighborhoods I otherwise never would have discovered. I spent hours outside instead of sitting behind a desk. Sometimes I listened to podcasts or music. Other times, I simply enjoyed the quiet.Those walks gave me space to think. I reflected on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.Before Rover, success meant getting promotions, landing bigger clients and climbing the corporate ladder. Walking dogs challenged that definition. I realized I didn't want to chase an impressive title as much as I wanted to chase a lifestyle that gave me energy.Ironically, it was during one of those walks that I received the phone call offering me the marketing job I still have today. I paused on the sidewalk, accepted the offer and then finished the walk.I put a photo of me and my husband holding our own pets (left) on my Rover profile. Long after my dog-walking era, I stayed friends with the dogs Tofu and Noodles (right) and their humans.Courtesy of Sally SimmonsReturning to marketing wasn't a difficult decision. By then, I was pregnant with my first daughter and needed the stability, benefits and predictable income that came with a full-time role. When an excited dog chasing a squirrel pulled me to the ground early in my pregnancy, it became clear that my season as a professional dog walker was coming to an end.Still, I think about those four months often. People sometimes assume dog walking was a gap or detour in my career. I see it as one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had.It reminded me that passion is visible, no matter what kind of work you're doing. It reinforced that the skills that matter most — showing up, listening, caring deeply, building trust and making small, consistent changes — translate to every career.And even though I'm back in marketing, my days look different than they did before my dog-walking era. These days, you'll find me logging off at 5 p.m. to go play outside with my family before dinner, walking near the ocean after a hard week, having kitchen dance parties to shake off the day, taking calls while walking my own dog or squeezing in a lunchtime workout. The fresh air and sense of presence give me the balance I craved when I was glued to screens on a schedule dictated by someone else's time zone.Those four months taught me something my MBA never could: Success isn't just about finding a job that sounds impressive. It's about building a life you genuinely enjoy living, even if it doesn't look like the one you originally imagined.Sally Simmons is a marketing leader and holistic health coach based in California. After years building strategies for global brands, she found unexpected lessons about business, connection and success during a four-month chapter as a professional dog walker. Today, she brings those lessons into her work helping people create healthier, more balanced lives.

schema.headline: I quit my marketing job to walk dogs for 4 months: It's 'one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had'

title: American embassies tighten security as Iran threat warnings intensify ahead of U.S. midterm elections
description: The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.AFP via Getty ImagesU.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East
body: The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.AFP via Getty ImagesU.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report, and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well. The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group Saturday, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu. Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June. Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal.The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high. U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel. watch now

schema.headline: American embassies tighten security as Iran threat warnings intensify ahead of U.S. midterm elections

title: Scalpers offer Apple iPhone Duo buyers hundreds extra outside Beijing launch
description: watch nowThe iPhone Duo has an eye-popping price tag, but initial interest in Apple's first foldable phone in China appears solid. On the day of the g
body: watch nowThe iPhone Duo has an eye-popping price tag, but initial interest in Apple's first foldable phone in China appears solid. On the day of the global launch on Friday, scalpers like Alex Wang stood outside the flagship store in Beijing's popular shopping area, Sanlitun, offering to pay customers an extra 3,000 Chinese yuan ($448) to buy their newly purchased phones on the spot.   "I feel the Duo can be sold with a higher price for half a month," he told CNBC while watching the lines of Duo customers who had pre-booked their phones. "The main reason is the tight supply."Though foldables are still a niche product globally, China's market is the single largest, according to Counterpoint Research.Apple fan Mary Tong, who was first in a line of about 100 people at the Sanlitun store, showed up at 6 a.m. to pick up her foldable device."Apple has been the laggard," she said. "I think many Chinese do prefer foldable phones."watch nowHuawei is promoting its own AI assistant XiaoYi to boost the Chinese smartphone maker's competitiveness against Apple and other homegrown rivals. Huawei, which already has a broad lineup of foldable phones, launched a new trifold called the Mate XT2 that is priced at about $3,000 on Sept. 7, two days before Apple's Duo announcement. China's Xiaomi unveiled its own pricey foldable, the 18 Fold, around the same time.Even before the Beijing Apple store's regular opening hours, customers without a reservation showed up to test their luck to get their hands on the new phone. Apple had said the Duo would not be available for walk-in purchase on launch day in mainland China and would be "limited" in other countries. Each online purchase was restricted to two phones.   Zhang Zheng said he had tried to order one on the site but was discouraged by the delivery timeline, which stretched to January 2027. He said he still wants to buy one. "I think it will be useful for work and it's cool to look at," he said.iPhone Duo smartphone sold at Apple Inc.'s Sanlitun store during the first day of in-store sales of the new device in Beijing, China, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. Stringer | Anadolu | Getty ImagesWhile there was buzz about the device itself, expectations for Apple Intelligence were negligible. The company said a version of the AI system is set for beta testing this month for the mainland China market and will include features like live translation, Clean Up in photos, and writing tools.On Oct. 14, Beijing approved Alibaba AI models for use in Duo and other Apple devices as part of the U.S. tech giant's pending AI rollout in the country. Apple received Chinese regulatory clearance over the summer.Chinese official media cited ex-CEO Tim Cook on a recent China trip as saying Apple's revamped Siri AI would not be available in the country yet.Duo customer John Zhao said he had tried Apple Intelligence while working overseas, and it was "nice but not beyond imagination." He expects the Chinese version to be less exciting.Read more CNBC tech newsMusk's clash with Ukraine accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives. title: What a day in customer service looks like — as AI changes everything
description: Maskot | Digitalvision | Getty ImagesFor Kaylee Harris, who works in customer service for a credit card company, a day at work now looks very differen
body: Maskot | Digitalvision | Getty ImagesFor Kaylee Harris, who works in customer service for a credit card company, a day at work now looks very different. Her hours used to be filled with calls, note-taking and lengthy card disclosures. Now, thanks to artificial intelligence, she can focus more on each customer, Harris told CNBC.For Shannon, AI has also changed things — but not in a good way. She works in customer service for a telecommunications company in Cardiff, Wales, and did not want to share her surname for fear of being identified by her employer. She told CNBC that AI-generated notes at her current workplace are often riddled with errors, "so I just write my own."At her previous employer, a property services company, senior management told staff to "ChatGPT it" if they didn't know the answer. AI agents booked appointments, but when they couldn't offer a customer the requested date, they passed the case to a human. Staff were "constantly fighting fires," Shannon said. "All the complicated cases came to us, causing a lot of burnout."Good for both employees and customers? In theory, automation in customer service should mean human agents spend less time on admin and more time helping customers with problems that require human judgment, empathy and experience.Nikola Mrkšić, CEO and co-founder of London-headquartered PolyAI, which develops voice AI systems for customer service, said contact-center agents can face "maximum abuse for minimum wage." They often deal with frustrated customers while working under strict performance metrics, sometimes without the authority or information to resolve problems, he told CNBC. He sees AI agents as a way to help shoulder that load.Maximum abuse for minimum wageNikola MrkšićPolyAI"It's a really, really difficult job," he said. "I think with AI, we have a shot at bridging the gap to make it better for both [customers and employees]."British telecom and media company Virgin Media O2 launched an AI voice agent in September, which it said was designed to do just that. The agent handles routine issues so human advisors can spend more time on complex or sensitive cases.At U.K.-based customer experience company ArvatoConnect, CEO Debra Maxwell told CNBC the company aims for 70% of interactions to be handled by technology and 30% by people. One AI tool it developed for the U.K. government's procurement agency, the Crown Commercial Service, generates draft supplier viability assessments with 97% accuracy, she said, reducing the need for hours of manual data extraction.The mental load of harder casesAs AI takes on routine tasks, human agents may be left dealing with a greater share of complicated cases — and be required to pick up the slack when the technology fails.The pressure on customer-service staff comes amid reports of rising workloads across the industry.According to MaxContact's 2025/26 U.K. Contact Centre KPI Benchmarking Insights Report, more than half of surveyed contact-center decision-makers said agent workloads had increased, up from around 40% in 2024, although the survey doesn't establish what is driving the rise.[R]elatively straightforward tasks can provide a bit of psychological respite between more demanding onesAmanda JonesKing's College LondonAmanda Jones, who researches organizational behavior and the future of work at King's College London, specializes in work intensification — the process by which jobs become more demanding over time. She told CNBC that AI could make call-center work even more intense if human agents are increasingly left with the toughest interactions."Some customers may already be frustrated by the time they reach that human," she said. "One thing we sometimes overlook is that relatively straightforward tasks can provide a bit of psychological respite between more demanding ones. If those disappear, the intensity of the working day could increase considerably, even if the overall volume of work doesn't."Jones cautioned that productivity gains may also bring more intense performance targets. And as routine tasks are automated, workers could lose opportunities to develop the experience needed for more demanding work."So, we could end up expecting people to perform more demanding work while simultaneously reducing the experiences that traditionally helped prepare them for it," she said.The human touchArvatoConnect's Maxwell argued that average handling times may need to increase as employees take on more complex cases."We assess whether [human] agents understood the customer's needs, exercised sound judgement and reached the right resolution," she said. "Not whether they followed a script or hit an arbitrary time target."Call center agent talking on a headset while working or assisting on computer screen in a office.Charday Penn | E+ | Getty ImagesHarris sees the upsides of AI tools, despite occasional system glitches that create more work. But she worries that the push to automate is coming, ultimately, at the expense of customer experience."As a country, I think we are focusing on getting things done faster and choosing quantity over quality … resulting in customers being fed up with the way AI is being pushed on everyone," she said.Shannon also sees the potential benefits of using AI, but doesn't think it should ever replace real customer service."I believe people buy from people; with AI you don't get to experience that," she said. "I go the extra mile. Can AI give that feeling? Can it feel genuine?"

schema.headline: What a day in customer service looks like — as AI changes everything

title: Musk's SpaceX is still restricting Starlink in Ukraine and the toll is rising
description: watch nowSpaceX's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a
body: watch nowSpaceX's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a national security expert said Friday."Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters," wrote Denys Sienik, Ukraine's deputy ambassador to the U.S., in a Friday post on X."Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives," Sienik said. "Unfortunately, as of today, nothing has changed. We continue to wait."Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said.Despite recent comments from President Donald Trump that indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade. "They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited."Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in the Zaporizhzhia region take a camouflage case off a Starlink satellite communication terminal to be set up at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, October 16, 2026. Dmytro Smolienko | Future Publishing | Getty ImagesUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on.""Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are." Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel."While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google.Elon Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear. Democratic lawmakers have since called for an investigation into Musk and the Starshield throttling. A group of bipartisan lawmakers penned a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday urging the agency to "act expeditiously to expand its Starshield arrangements and ensure uninterrupted satellite communications support for Ukraine." The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump spoke to Musk by phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals. Trump said Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back."But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored. "I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him."Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service.Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors." On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed a letter of intent with Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release. "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."-- CNBC's Eamon Javers and Lora Kolodny contributed reporting to this story.Read more CNBC tech newsMusk's clash with Ukraine accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives. title: Fact vs. fiction: Doctors share whether peptides are safe and effective
description: From YouTube influencers to Reddit threads, the health and wellness side of the internet is full of talk about peptides.The term refers to a class of
body: From YouTube influencers to Reddit threads, the health and wellness side of the internet is full of talk about peptides.The term refers to a class of chemical compounds made up of short chains of amino acids. In the wellness market, synthetic peptides are often sold to consumers as injectables, which some health influencers say can bring a wide range of health benefits from muscle recovery and longevity to improved sexual function. Some peptides, including GLP-1 drugs commonly used for weight loss or diabetes, are heavily researched and federally approved for medical use. Many other forms of peptides are not.Yet even some lightly researched peptides may be on their way to pharmacy shelves. The Department of Health and Human Services is reportedly planning to allow specialty pharmacies to compound certain synthetic peptides that have the support of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who told podcaster Joe Rogan that he is a "big fan" of the injectables in a February 2026 interview. As reported, the move would be an interim access policy covering some specific peptides not currently approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.Such a move would be controversial from a regulatory point of view: Multiple peptides, including one of the compounds reportedly included in the health department's proposal, appear on an FDA list of injectables that "may present significant safety risks." That compound, known as BPC-157, has shown potential anti-inflammatory effects in some animal and lab studies but has not yet been subject to large-scale human testing for safety or effectiveness."There are a few reasons why, but one of the main ones is the absence of evidence," including robust human studies on safety and effectiveness, says Dr. Caleb Alexander, a professor of epidemiology and medicine at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.Yet consumer interest and regulatory momentum for peptides are growing. So here's what you need to know about peptides, from why they're the subject of such conversation to whether or not they're safe or effective to use.What are peptides?Peptides are "kind of like the building blocks of proteins," says Dr. Alison Dempsey, a dermatologist at the Weill Cornell Medicine and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital.Several different types of peptides are naturally found in the body, like insulin and endorphins. Peptides can also be synthesized in labs, according to Harvard Health Publishing. GLP-1s, like Ozempic, are FDA-approved synthetic peptides, Dempsey says.Injectable variations of synthetic peptides that haven't been approved by the FDA — such as BPC-157 and GHK-Cu, the latter of which has been marketed as a potential anti-aging drug — are the peptides that are making headlines at the moment, says Dr. Pieter Cohen, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School and internist at Cambridge Health Alliance.Why are peptides gaining popularity among wellness influencers and some other consumers?One likely factor behind synthetic peptides gaining more attention has been the success of drugs like Ozempic at addressing health concerns such as obesity and diabetes, according to Cohen. "That probably opened up [the idea that] there must be this magical world of these other peptides that we can have access to, that will do these sort of similar magical things in other areas," he says.However, Cohen and other health experts have their concerns. After all, a compound's status as a peptide "doesn't mean it's close to Ozempic in any way, shape or form ... in terms of both its chemical structure or its effects on the human body," says Cohen.Synthetic peptides advertised on social media and sold on the so-called gray market — often produced by overseas sellers and sold to U.S. consumers outside the normal American drug regulatory system — come with marketing claims such as boosting longevity, improving sleep quality, strengthening the immune system and even enhancing skin health and sexual function, according to Alexander.Particularly among the people who consider GLP-1s a form of miracle drug, consumers may simply want to believe that the weight loss medicine's chemical cousins could have similar effects on other elements of human health. "Unfortunately, when it comes to peptides marketing, word of mouth has strongly surpassed where we are with any type of research," Dempsey says.What do health experts recommend for consumers?The health experts who spoke with CNBC Make It recommend against using any injectable peptides that aren't approved by the FDA, especially if you're unsure where or how they were produced. Always consult with a medical professional before making any major changes that can affect your health."My recommendation is not to use any of the novel, unstudied injectable peptides because we simply do not know if they work. And if they do work, if they're safe," Cohen says. When buying peptides on the gray market, you can receive entirely different compounds or doses, and some may be contaminated with bacteria or other concerning materials, he says."There's concerns both about the potential risks, but also about the unclear level of benefit from these products," Alexander says."We have a great regulatory system governing prescription drugs in the United States," Alexander adds. "For advocates of these products that really believe in them, I hope that they'll put their money where their mouth is, and do the studies that are necessary so that we can understand the true safety and effectiveness of the products."

schema.headline: Fact vs. fiction: Doctors share whether peptides are safe and effective

title: An ex-bookkeeper spent $375 to launch a sewing business: 'I hadn't felt so sure about something like that in a long time'
description: Eric Lugo didn't know that when he launched his sewing workshop business, Stitch Lab ATX, as a side project in May 2025, it'd become his full-time foc
body: Eric Lugo didn't know that when he launched his sewing workshop business, Stitch Lab ATX, as a side project in May 2025, it'd become his full-time focus within weeks.Lugo also couldn't have predicted it'd become so successful within two years that offerings would grow fivefold, classes would regularly sell out and he'd start getting requests to host private events.The idea came to him a few years ago: Lugo learned to sew from his grandma when he was 5 and got serious about it as a teen, eventually launching his fashion brand, Casa Amiré, and becoming his friends' go-to guy for tailoring and alterations help. Dresses needed hemming, jeans needed shortening. Lugo was happy to lend his talents, though the requests piled up.So one day, in April 2024, he thought: What if he taught his friends how to fix their clothes themselves?"It really made me think: Wow, this is — I think — a pretty important skill that a lot of people don't know how to do," Lugo, 29, of Austin, Texas, tells CNBC Make It. He could fill that gap. "I think I have enough knowledge after you know 14 [or] 15 years to be able to teach other people, and so I went from there."A $375 investmentFor months, while in between jobs and selling wares from his fashion brand, Lugo couldn't stop thinking about launching a sewing workshop. Around August 2024, he got a bookkeeping job for a local PR firm and shelved the idea. But by the beginning of 2025, it was back on his mind. He mapped out the classes he'd offer and how he'd get the word out.By April, Lugo put money into it. He spent $375 to buy eight sewing machines, sourced second-hand from Facebook Marketplace, and set up shop in a friend's warehouse space that wasn't in use outside of business hours. Lugo gathered friends and family members to test-run his curriculum.Stitch Lab ATX held its first classes in early May, Lugo says, with a few sign-ups for one-on-one private lessons and a handful of students taking his "crash course" workshop covering beginner-friendly basics, like learning how to thread a machine and sewing a straight line. Then Lugo's circumstances changed fast: Toward the end of May, he was let go from his day job. It wasn't a question that he'd go all-in on his studio."Not even 10 minutes after I had just gotten laid off and gotten off of that Zoom meeting, I called my boy that has the warehouse, and I said, 'Dude, I just got laid off. Are you cool with me just going full-send with Stitch Lab?'" Lugo says. His friend was 100% in."I honestly hadn't felt so sure about something like that in a long time, if ever," Lugo says.A rise in DIY hobbiesIt took some time for things to get moving.By his count, Lugo held around four to six classes in those early months. Sometimes just two or three people would show up, even though he could host up to 10. Lugo says demand picked up around September 2025 once he started partnering with local businesses to host pop-up sewing events (like a sip-and-stitch at a brewery) and spreading the word on TikTok.Eric Lugo started Stitch Lab ATX after spending $375 on eight second-hand sewing machines sourced from Facebook Marketplace.Courtesy of Eric LugoToday the lab offers around two dozen classes per month and can fill up quickly when spots open up a month in advance, Lugo says. Sessions typically cost $65 to $85 and last about two-and-a-half hours. Classes range from beginner-friendly lessons, like learning how to use a machine, to teaching intermediate skills, like hemming pants or installing a zipper. Students can sign up for special workshops to make a specific project, like a flower tote, or book open sewing time at the warehouse space. Lugo also takes requests to teach at special events, like for a bachelorette party or corporate offsite, averaging about one a month.Lugo says he draws a salary from the business, which is his primary source of income.Stitch Lab's success coincides with a trend of many Americans paying up to invest in their hobbies, even as the costs of goods and materials rise, leading to a trend of what Bank of America refers to as "funflation." Spending on hobbies, ranging from arts and crafts and hobby shops to retailers selling skiing, hiking, camping or scuba diving gear, grew 7.9% in August 2026 from the year prior, according to the bank's analysis of its card data.Stitch Lab ATX offers about two dozen classes per month and hosts private workshops for groups like bachelorette parties and corporate retreats.To help some students offset these costs, Lugo in August began a monthly giveaway initiative called Sew It Forward, where entrants can comment on a Stitch Lab social media post about why they want to learn to sew, for the chance to win a free new sewing machine, supplies and a free class with the studio."I'm thankful for the support that I've received," Lugo says, "and so I want to put all that back into the community now that I'm in a position to do so."A growing sewing communityStitch Lab also stands out during a time when people, especially young adults, are craving community-oriented, offline social events. There's even a resurgence of so-called "grandma hobbies," like knitting and scrapbooking, as people seek relaxing pastimes that keep them off their phones. In the warehouse dotted with sewing machines and early 2000s or reggaeton music streaming from the sound system, Lugo says he aims to build Stitch Lab up as a fun, creative "judgment-free zone" that can "feel like a home for people."As an Afro-Latino founder, he says, "this is a safe space for Latinos, for people of color.""I think community is needed, especially today with so much that's happening in the world," he adds. "No matter who you are, where you come from, you have a safe space to be around other people, learn the same thing ... and just have fun."Eric Lugo learned to sew from his grandma when he was 5. He got serious about it as a teenager and launched his own fashion brand, Casa Amiré.Courtesy of Eric LugoStitch Lab ATX's future plans are already taking shape. Lugo says he just hired two part-time instructors to his team, which will allow them to expand to upward of 30 workshops per month. He still aims to keep classes relatively intimate to support one-on-one help and small-group socializing.Lugo even sees his business expanding beyond Austin, with his sights set on New York City, hotspots across California and even Mexico City."I just want to continue to do what I'm doing all around the world," he says.

title: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating as country grapples with turmoil and higher yields
description: A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration as part of a nationwide mobilization over rising living costs, fuel prices and education fundin
body: A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration as part of a nationwide mobilization over rising living costs, fuel prices and education funding in Paris, France, on Oct. 17, 2026.Ibrahim Ezzat | Anadolu | Getty ImagesMoody's opted to maintain its credit rating on France as the country contended with a week of civil unrest and rising political risk.The agency kept France's credit rating at Aa3, a level Moody's still deems "high grade," but it also maintained its negative outlook on the nation."The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report. Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow the deficit. Investors were anticipating Moody's rating decision as France, the second-largest economy in the euro zone, grappled with protests and a sharp surge in bond yields. "This political instability, also visible in the current social tensions, risks hampering the French government's ability to address key policy challenges such as an elevated fiscal deficit, rising debt burden, and durable increase in borrowing costs, thus leading to a more rapid weakening in the sovereign's key credit metrics than we currently expect," Moody's said in its report Friday.This week, the nation's 10-year bond yield surpassed 5% for the first time since 2002. The spread against German bunds is also at a 15-year peak. Currently, France's deficit-to-GDP ratio is at roughly 5.5% of its GDP, sharply above the 3% limit for member nations in the European Union. The country faces more than $1 trillion of debt that will mature by 2030. Just a month ago, the French finance ministry warned that the nation's debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to hit 121.7% in 2027.At the same time, France has been rocked by protests. Last weekend, more than 500,000 people marched to express their frustration against declining public services and high costs of living. S&P Global and Fitch cut their ratings on France in 2025.

schema.headline: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating as country grapples with turmoil and higher yields

title: Trump dropping some Canada tariffs but 'replacing' them with other products
description: The White House on Friday said it would drop tariffs on some Canadian goods, but replace them with other products from the major U.S. trade partner.Th
body: The White House on Friday said it would drop tariffs on some Canadian goods, but replace them with other products from the major U.S. trade partner.The move was revealed after Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, took credit for pushing the Trump administration to issue tariff exemptions on several categories of Canadian imports she says are "crucial" for her state's industries.But Collins' announcement, which The Wall Street Journal first reported, did not mention that while tariffs would be removed for some Canadian products, new ones would be added to the list of goods subject to steep U.S. duties. The White House announced the new tariffs less than an hour after Collins touted the new exemptions to the tariffs, which are unpopular in the state where she's fighting for reelection.President Donald Trump earlier Friday signed a proclamation "removing certain products" from the list of items that he slapped 50% tariffs on over the summer using a 96-year-old trade law.But he is "replacing those products with certain valves, carpets, waste products, and others," according to a White House fact sheet detailing the proclamation.The changes are being made to "further refine the scope of the tariffs on certain Canadian products," according to the fact sheet, which does not mention Maine.The new additions and removals from the list of goods covered by the "Section 338" tariffs will take effect Oct. 30, four days before the Nov. 3 U.S. election, the fact sheet said.Asked what Collins had agreed to in her conversations pushing Trump administration officials for lower tariffs on products affecting her state, her spokeswoman Phoebe Keller told CNBC that the senator "requested exemptions for products that are important to Maine and will continue to do so."Before the fact sheet was made public, Collins' office sent a press release crediting the senator with securing the new tariff exemptions on "nine categories of products crucial for Maine's agricultural industries."That announcement came as voters have already started casting ballots in the pivotal Maine Senate race, where Trump's unpopular tariffs have been a top issue.Collins' Democratic opponent, fifth-generation Maine logger Troy Jackson, quickly pushed back, insisting  Collins deserves blame for enabling Trump's tariff policies."Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire," Jackson said in a statement. Trump has slapped heavy tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods during his second term as president as he has escalated a trade war against the top U.S. economic partner. Many of those tariffs have put considerable strain on businesses in Maine, which imports far more products from Canada than from any other country.White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC in a statement Friday afternoon that Trump's latest tariff proclamation is part of his efforts to "address Canada's discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce.""The President is taking action in response to Canada's continued discrimination against and additional retaliation targeting U.S. commerce, with the goal of protecting American farmers, manufacturers, and workers," said Middleton. "This administration will continue to use every available tool to restore reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships and safeguard the economic prosperity and national security of the American people."Collins has previously touted her efforts to push back on the president's protectionist trade policies. In the first televised debate between Collins and Jackson on Oct. 6, the GOP incumbent took credit for removing some items from Trump's list of tariffs on Canadian goods, including road salt.Jackson fired back, "What about everything else? We can't eat road salt."In her press release Friday, Collins said she has asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "for tariff relief" for the Maine-centric products, stressing the "burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families.""I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally and largest trading partner," she said.According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Mexico is the largest U.S. trading partner.The products being exempted from the Section 338 tariffs include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and packing bags, refrigeration equipment, multiple forms of machinery and seaweed and algae products, according to Collins.

title: Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield high speed restrictions have been lifted
description: A Ukrainian soldier of the 61st Separate Mechanized Brigade uses the Starlink system during military exercises in the Chernihiv region, Ukraine, June
body: A Ukrainian soldier of the 61st Separate Mechanized Brigade uses the Starlink system during military exercises in the Chernihiv region, Ukraine, June 2023 (Photo by Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesUkraine said Saturday that high-speed service has been restored for SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems, a day after declaring that they remained throttled. Ukrainian official said the service disruption left the country vulnerable to Russian attacks."The monitoring systems of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine officially record the restoration of the speed of Starlink/Starshield," it said in a statement. "The connection remains stable [while equipment is moving] at speeds over 400 km/h (249 miles per hour)." "Previously, monitoring systems recorded limitations in the operation of Starlink/Starshield. Now the speed indicators have been restored," the ministry added.Starlink is SpaceX's broader commercial satellite internet network, while Starshield is the company's government operations built on Starlink technology. SpaceX did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.A soldier from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine uses a smartphone to check signal quality while setting up a Starlink satellite communication network at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, on October 16, 2026. Dmytro Smolienko | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesSince Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade offering of its Starlink satellite internet service. Officials said any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions.Despite recent comments from U.S. President Donald Trump indicating service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade.'Things have become harder'Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on.""Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are."Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said it continues to monitor the systems' operations."This result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," Defense Minister Yevgeny Khmara said in the statement.Lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties have called for a formal probe into Musk and SpaceX over alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine.

schema.headline: Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield high speed restrictions have been lifted

title: What next for France as riots rattle markets? Three questions facing investors ahead of more protests
description: France's unrest is fueling investor concerns over the country's fiscal outlook, after borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2002 earlier this
body: France's unrest is fueling investor concerns over the country's fiscal outlook, after borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2002 earlier this week.With further demonstrations planned, fund managers are assessing whether prolonged disruption could weaken growth, undermine confidence and make it harder for the government to deliver planned budget savings.Rating agency Moody's on Friday kept its Aa3 credit rating on France, a level it still deems "high grade," but maintained its negative outlook on the nation."The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report.Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow its budget deficit.watch nowCan France's government pass its budget?France's government aims to reduce the budget deficit to 5% of GDP in 2027, from a projected 5.4% in 2026. The National Assembly is due to resume debating on the budget's tax measures, which are intended to generate savings, on Oct. 27 but opposition lawmakers are resisting the plans.Alain Durré, head of EMEA economic research at Natixis CIB, said the government was determined to prevent a sharp rise in borrowing costs.Durré said the government could try to stick to its fiscal targets by invoking Article 49.3 — which allows it to push a bill through the assembly without a final vote unless lawmakers can pass a no-confidence motion — or by using executive ordinances.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconFrance 10-Year OATs.That could help settle nerves and restore investor confidence, Durré added, noting that recent pressure on French sovereign debt has been driven primarily by tactical portfolio reallocations, with traditional buy-and-hold investors "still sitting on the sidelines."The yield on benchmark 10-year French government bonds, known as OATs, climbed 11 basis points Thursday to its highest level since 2002. That pushed the spread over 10-year German Bunds — the benchmark for euro zone debt — to its widest level since November 2011.Charlotte de Montpellier, senior economist for France and Switzerland at ING, said the unrest "adds another layer of uncertainty" to the budgetary and political concerns already weighing on French assets, and "reinforces the perception that any future government will find it difficult to deliver the reforms and savings required.""It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament," said Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at Ebury. "Even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed."What damage will the unrest do to France's growth outlook?Fresh demonstrations are planned for Oct. 24, and a union-backed national day of strikes and protests is set for Nov. 5, with anti-establishment Yellow Vest protestors among those calling for further rallies.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCAC 40.In a note on Oct. 20 after the violence of the previous weekend, de Montpellier said that, while the market can look past short-lived disruption, "a lasting loss of confidence can have a bigger impact.""These events further darken an economic outlook that was already unfavorable," she said. "We had expected French GDP growth of just 0.3% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027. If the unrest continues, confidence deteriorates further or market tensions intensify, growth could be even weaker."The Yellow Vest movement may have reduced French GDP growth in the fourth quarter of 2018 by 0.1 percentage point, according to an INSEE estimate cited by de Montpellier. Industrial action during the spring 2023 pension protests reduced first-quarter GDP growth by around 0.1 percentage point, according to the Banque de France.In her Oct. 20 note, she said violence could keep households away from city centers and prompt tourists to postpone trips and businesses to delay investment. watch nowDurré said French consumer sentiment was already near historic lows before the latest protests, leaving little room for the country to absorb a fresh macroeconomic shock.He added the unrest raises "two key red flags" for markets."First, the risk that prolonged disruption drags on GDP growth. Second, fears that political pressure could derail government plans for critical spending cuts ... Either way, that would widen the deficit and blow past the government's 5% GDP target."Which French sectors are most exposed?France's CAC 40 has fallen 4.5% over the past month. ING identified retail, hospitality and tourism, and transport and logistics as the sectors most directly exposed to the turmoil.De Montpellier said shops and shopping centers face lower footfall, closures and lost sales; hotels, cafés, restaurants and travel services risk losing activity that customers are less likely to reschedule. Transport and logistics could also be hit if disruption persists, she added.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCarrefour.Carrefour shares plunged more than 14% Wednesday after the supermarket giant cut its profit outlook and reduced investment, citing the unrest — along with rising energy costs — as a drag on consumer sentiment. CEO Alexandre Bompard said the country faces an "unprecedented situation."More than 2,000 businesses had been directly affected by Tuesday, ING said, citing estimates from France's network of chambers of commerce.The impact could extend well beyond companies most directly exposed to the unrest, said Kevin Thozet, portfolio advisor and member of the investment committee at Carmignac.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconLVMH."For equities, this does not help banks, given the higher cost of equity, while prolonged uncertainty can slow loan growth and create credit problems," he told CNBC via email.France's prestigious luxury sector generates most of its sales abroad. LVMH has relatively limited direct exposure to the French market, with France accounting for just 8% of its 2025 revenue. But the demonstrations could weigh on tourism and therefore tax-free purchases, which account for around 20% of LVMH's revenue in France, Thozet said."A further six months of political vacuum is a very long time for markets, the economy and entrepreneurs," he added.

schema.headline: What next for France as riots rattle markets? Three questions facing investors ahead of more protests

title: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
description: The Amgen logo is displayed outside Amgen headquarters in Thousand Oaks, California, on May 17, 2023.Mario Tama | Getty ImagesA drug from Amgen could
body: The Amgen logo is displayed outside Amgen headquarters in Thousand Oaks, California, on May 17, 2023.Mario Tama | Getty ImagesA drug from Amgen could give patients with a notoriously aggressive form of lung cancer significantly more time to live when added to an immunotherapy from AstraZeneca, a study found.Full results from a late-stage trial released Saturday show that adding Amgen's immunotherapy Imdelltra to AstraZeneca's Imfinzi drug slashed the risk of death by 58% in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, a fast-growing disease that has spread beyond the lung where it began.The drug combination extended their median overall survival to 21.1 months compared with 12.7 months with AstraZeneca's drug alone, the trial found.That means half of patients in the group that took the combination regimen were alive for at least roughly 21 months. The trial tested the combo as a maintenance therapy in patients who received initial treatment with Imfinzi and chemotherapy, and whose cancer had not progressed."I think there are moments in medicine when you see a piece of data that is so profound that it's going to transform the standard of care for patients, and I think, honestly, we're at that moment," said Dr. Paul Burton, Amgen's chief medical officer, in an interview.The combination "has the potential to take on one of the most aggressive cancers that we deal with today, and almost convert it into a chronic disease," he said, adding that "these data say that's a possibility." The results also suggest a greater commercial opportunity for Imdelltra, which posted $288 million in sales during the second quarter, up 115% year over year. The drug already generated $627 million in global sales in 2025 and appears to be on its way to becoming a blockbuster medicine, or hitting the $1 billion sales threshold.Small cell lung cancer remains difficult to treat because, even if chemotherapy initially works well for most patients, the disease often returns or progresses within months, said lead trial investigator Dr. Jacob Sands, who is the associate chief of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. He said immunotherapy has helped a small subset of patients achieve years of disease control, but most have not experienced similarly durable benefits, highlighting the need for better treatments. There are roughly 31,000 new small cell lung cancer cases in the U.S. each year, and an estimated 60% to 70% of those people are diagnosed with extensive-stage disease.Sands said the benefits in the trial were seen across subgroups of patients, including those whose cancer spread to the brain or liver. Disease that has spread to those organs is associated with poorer treatment outcomes.He added that with longer-term follow-up data on the patients, the 21-month figure "may evolve further and hopefully will substantially improve," similar to what Amgen saw in a Phase 1 trial on the immunotherapy combination. In that early-stage trial on a smaller number of patients, a long-term follow-up showed the benefit was sustained for years. Using Imdelltra earlier Amgen said the findings also suggest that using Imdelltra earlier in a patient's treatment could meaningfully alter the trajectory of the disease. Imdelltra is currently approved for patients whose small cell lung cancer has progressed while they are on, or after, platinum-based chemotherapy.Researchers specifically tested whether adding Imdelltra could help patients live longer than continuing Imfinzi alone, which is already approved as a first treatment for this type of lung cancer. Amgen said nearly 80% of patients who started taking both drugs were alive at one year compared with 53% receiving Imfinzi alone. Imdelltra's "big impact" on controlling the disease and ultimately how long people live highlights the importance of including it in first-line maintenance treatment, Sands said. That refers to ongoing therapy given after an initial heavy treatment, such as chemotherapy or surgery.Burton added that it positions Amgen's drug to be an "indispensable backbone therapy" for small cell lung cancer, regardless of the other immunotherapy that can be paired with it. Imdelltra binds to DLL3, a protein on cancer cells, and CD3, a protein on T cells, which are a type of immune cell that can kill cancer. By binding to both, Imdelltra brings T cells into close contact with tumor cells, helping the immune system destroy the cancer. Imfinzi, made by AstraZeneca, is an immunotherapy that blocks a protein called PD-L1, which cancer cells use to evade the immune system. The drugs work together in complementary ways: Imfinzi helps remove the brakes on the immune response, while Imdelltra brings T cells directly to cancer cells and helps activate them to attack the tumor.The study, which was presented at a major cancer meeting called the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, did not test whether the combination was better than other first-line treatment approaches. Still, the findings suggest Amgen's drug could be another option offered to small cell lung cancer patients earlier in their treatment. Kate Brenan, a 44-year-old mother of two from Denver, sees that as a win on its own. She was diagnosed with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in early January 2024. Brenan underwent six rounds of a common combination chemotherapy, followed by chest radiation and later whole-brain radiation after the cancer spread. In September 2024, she started Imdelltra and has had no evidence of disease ever since. "I think that it's remarkable how quickly things are changing in the world of small cancer treatment options," Brenan told CNBC, adding that Imdelltra potentially becoming an earlier treatment option "can only be a good thing for the patients moving forward, and I'm really excited about that."

schema.headline: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer

title: Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war has redrawn global energy markets
description: watch nowBefore the Iran war, Qatar was one of the biggest natural gas exporters in the world. After only eight months, the Gulf state is now buying s
body: watch nowBefore the Iran war, Qatar was one of the biggest natural gas exporters in the world. After only eight months, the Gulf state is now buying supplies from its principal competitor — the United States. QatarEnergy struck a deal Thursday with U.S. exporter Cheniere Energy to buy 4 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, annually through 2054. The purchase price is indexed to the U.S. Henry Hub price plus a fixed fee. Deliveries are expected to begin in the 2030s. "We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century," Cheniere CEO Jack Fusco said in a statement. The gas that Doha will buy is less than 1% of the global LNG trade of more than 400 million metric tons. But "in terms of an individual deal, this is about as big as you see in the U.S," said Alex Munton, director of global gas and LNG at Rapidan Energy in Houston.The deal signals how the Iran war is reshaping global energy markets to the benefit of U.S. companies, cementing the dominance of American LNG exporters. Shares of Cheniere and Venture Global, the other independent U.S. player, have gained 26% and 40%, respectively, since the start of the war. Qatar knocked outQatar was second only to the U.S. in LNG exports before the war. But shipments have since collapsed in the eight months since Iran bombed its key production facility at Ras Laffan. The attack badly damaged two production lines, taking out about 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity.It will take about three years to repair the damage at Ras Laffan, Qatar's energy minister, Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, has said. The Persian Gulf state has declared force majeure — citing unexpected, uncontrollable events preventing contracts from being honored — every month since the March attack."It did give us a big blow, if you will, for our production capability for the next few years," Al-Kaabi said in an interview on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in September. Qatar is exporting "very little" LNG right now because "we can't export through the Hormuz Strait," he said."Very sparingly, some ships are crossing the straits but a very small amount, it's not something that would even be measurable in a percentage point," the energy minister said. Freedom of navigationAnd it is far from clear what security conditions in Hormuz will look like when the repairs are done at Ras Laffan. The decades-long contract with Cheniere indicates that Qatar sees a risk that freedom of navigation will never return to Hormuz as Iran keeps attacking tankers, Munton said. It is harder to find ways to get around Hormuz in the case of LNG because it is fundamentally a waterborne product, the analyst said. "It's liquefied so it can be put on a ship and that requires access to seaborne routes," Munton said. "They've got to access the Strait of Hormuz. There's no other way of getting LNG to market. They're just stuck."With its production badly damaged and Hormuz blocked off, QatarEnergy is expanding its LNG trading business through the Cheniere deal, Munton said. It secured a $3 billion loan earlier this month from Chinese banks that could allow it to secure more U.S. LNG to honor its international delivery commitments, said Manav Gupta, a UBS analyst, in a note to clients Thursday. Bullish Wall StreetVenture Global, for example, is in advanced talks with QatarEnergy to supply 3 million metric tons annually, unnamed sources told Reuters. With the Qatar deal, Cheniere is disproving the bears' case that it will struggle to secure incremental sales which would in turn constrain capacity expansion, Gupta said. UBS has a stock price target of $340 on Cheniere, implying 18% upside from Thursday's close. Wall Street is broadly bullish on both Cheniere and Venture Global. Nearly 90% of equity analysts who cover Cheniere rate it a buy, with an average price target of $314, implying about 9% upside from Thursday's close. Nearly 60% of analysts recommend Venture Global as a buy with the rest rating it a hold. The average  price target of $17 would amount to some 35% upside from Thursday's close. "The U.S. once again is being called on by buyers to diversify supply," Munton said. "So much is under construction in the U.S. that you get to the point where now the U.S. is becoming disproportionately big in terms of global [LNG] market share."

schema.headline: Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war has redrawn global energy markets

title: TikTok U.S. hunts for multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources tell CNBC
description: TikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC, amid a global scramble for digital infrastructu
body: TikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC, amid a global scramble for digital infrastructure deals. The company, officially TikTok USDS Joint Venture, operates the social media platform in the U.S. and has sounded out opportunities to obtain capacity over the coming years, two people familiar with the discussions, who asked to remain anonymous as they weren't authorized to share the information, told CNBC.TikTok U.S. is looking for four gigawatts of compute power by the early 2030s, one source said.Companies across the world are looking to secure more compute capacity as artificial intelligence workloads become more prominent. A company spokesperson told CNBC that the company "runs primarily on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in the U.S. and Oracle will continue to be our primary cloud infrastructure provider."Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI, typically runs in facilities that Oracle leases. CNBC has approached Oracle for comment.There are signs TikTok U.S.' product plans could require extra compute going forward. The company has numerous machine learning roles live on its website. A job advert posted by TikTok states that the company is "shipping a flagship B2B AI product at the frontier of large-model inference and creative automation."TikTok U.S. localizes algorithm trainingTikTok USDS Joint Venture was established in 2026 in compliance with U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order mandating the divestiture of TikTok in the U.S. from its Chinese parent company, ByteDance. In January, TikTok U.S. said it would "retrain, test, and update" its prized recommendation algorithm, which is built on machine learning, on U.S. user data. The company's recommendation algorithm will be "secured in Oracle's U.S. cloud environment," it said.TikTok U.S. has three managing investors, Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX, each holding 15%. The Dell Family Office, the investment firm of Michael Dell, is also an investor. ByteDance retained 19.9% of the new entity.

schema.headline: TikTok U.S. hunts for multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources tell CNBC
